transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. 

Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just keep messing up little things. It's nothing major, but it's getting frustrating. Like, I'll write the wrong time down on a sign-up sheet for a class at the senior center. Or I'll be working on a project and measure a board, but I still end up cutting it a hair short because I just sort of skipped over the small print or the little lines. It's just constant little careless mistakes like that.
Looking back at your life, did you experience these kinds of careless mistakes and difficulties with attention when you were a child, or is this a newer development?

No, it's... it's definitely not a new thing. Going all the way back, even in elementary school, I remember my teachers writing on my report cards that I was a bright kid, but I'd always forget my books or end up losing my homework. They said I'd just stare out the window most of the time, unless someone was right there to keep me on track. So, yeah, it's been this way pretty much my whole life.
When you are in situations where you are expected to remain seated for long periods, do you often find yourself feeling restless or fidgety?

Yeah, I'd say so. If I have to sit through a whole meeting, or... or even just during a quiet evening at the condo, I start getting this ants-in-my-pants feeling. I just want to get up, check on something, or putter around a bit instead of just sitting there.
In your daily life, do you often find yourself talking excessively or interrupting others when they are in the middle of a sentence?

No, I wouldn't say so. I'm actually pretty quiet most of the time. I don't really... talk people's ears off or jump in when they're in the middle of saying something. If anything, I'm usually just sitting back and letting them talk.

When you feel that restlessness during meetings or at home, do you find that it is so strong that you feel you absolutely must get up and move around, or is it more of a mild internal feeling of discomfort?

It's... well, it's more of just a mild discomfort. I don't feel like I absolutely have to jump up right that second or anything. It's just a bit of a nagging feeling, you know, where I'd really rather be up doing something else, but I can usually stay put if I really need to.
